1. Executive Summary & Application Profile

What the numbers say

  • The workload is compute‑bound: the core‑busy ratio is high (0.911) and the IPC comfortably exceeds 1.0.
  • There is moderate backend pressure (≈ 38 % of slots stalled on execution resources), while the frontend is relatively benign.
  • The memory subsystem shows a small working‑set that largely resides in L1/L2, with only ~9 % of L1 accesses falling to L2 and virtually no L3 traffic.
  • The main contention comes from backend stalls and a noticeable branch‑mis‑prediction cost, particularly for indirect branches.

No execution phases or core‑level utilization anomalies appear in the raw telemetry; the process runs steadily, keeping the majority of cores busy throughout the 5‑minute interval.

2. Top‑Down Microarchitectural Analysis

The top‑down breakdown (from the amdtopdown group) is:

> Primary bottleneck: Backend‑bound stalls dominate the pipeline (≈ 44 % of this thread’s own slots). > The high backend utilization reflects that the processor is frequently waiting on execution resources, most notably memory‑dependent operations (see cache‑miss data below).

Branch‑misprediction

  • IBS reports 8.1 % of branch‑retiring ops mispredicted.

3. Memory & Cache Subsystem Behavior

Implication: The application’s data footprint is small enough to avoid L3 cache pressure but still large enough that ~10 % of L1 data accesses must go to L2 and a substantial portion ultimately reaches DRAM. The backend stalls seen in the top‑down view are consistent with these memory‑bound delays.

4. Conclusion & Actionable Recommendations

Overall assessment Stockfish, as compiled with GCC O3 and default tuning, achieves a solid IPC of 1.11 on a 2.78 GHz Zen‑4 core and keeps the majority of cores busy (0.911 core‑busy). The main performance impediment is backend execution stall, driven by moderate L2 miss activity and a non‑negligible fraction of memory accesses reaching DRAM. Branch misprediction, especially on indirect branches, also contributes a measurable cost but is secondary to memory‑related stalls.

Applying the above recommendations—particularly focusing on data‑layout changes and compiler‑enabled vectorization—will likely yield the most significant performance gains for this workload.
